  CRT hardware, into software emulation, remote session multiplexing, and finally
  GPU-accelerated modern applications, is a study in how interfaces persist by adapting their
  implementation while preserving their essential interaction model. At no point in this
  history did anyone design "the terminal" as a coherent, planned system. Instead, each
  generation solved the specific problems facing it, printing without paper, moving a cursor
  efficiently, achieving portability across incompatible hardware, surviving unreliable
  networks, rendering text faster, while remaining compatible with decades of accumulated
  software built atop earlier assumptions.

  This compatibility constraint, more than any single technical virtue, explains the
  terminal's remarkable longevity. A text editor written to work with VT100 escape sequences
  in 1980 can still function, largely unmodified, in a GPU-accelerated terminal emulator
  running on hardware inconceivable to its original author. Few interfaces in computing can
  claim that kind of continuity, and it is precisely this unbroken chain of backward
  compatibility, layered incrementally atop a decades-old foundation, that explains why the
  terminal, seemingly the most anachronistic interface in modern computing, remains not just
  alive but actively developed, refined, and preferred by millions of engineers today.

⏺ A History of ANSI Escape Codes

  Introduction

  ANSI escape codes are one of the most quietly persistent standards in computing. Embedded
  in nearly every terminal emulator, shell prompt, and command-line tool in use today, they
  trace their origins to a standardization effort that predates personal computing itself.
  Their history is not the story of a single inventor or a single elegant design decision,
